edition.title: Slow Burn - Thursday 12 November 2026
edition.fact: Edition 38. The tide and the boardroom. Thursday 12 November 2026, edition 38. This edition runs 5,415 words. The day after America's hot inflation print, Dalal Street sprinted: the Sensex rose 772.75 points to 81,879.40 and the Nifty 210.40 points to 25,255.05, its highest close since February, and foreigners bought Rs 12,563 crore - the third-biggest daily inflow of 2026 ; foreigners have been net buyers in most November sessions. New York had already answered: CoreWeave's beat-and-raise lifted it 24.71% and carried the Nasdaq up 1.6%, Europe to a record close. Overnight the story turned to the boardroom: Nvidia's board met Wednesday to decide whether to oust Jensen Huang - Reuters confirming the Wall Street Journal's report with its own source - and the stock slid about 8% after hours. India's own October inflation print lands this afternoon - polls see it breaching 6% for the first time in two years. Abu Dhabi ended with the war's biggest prisoner exchange agreed in principle; the American envoys are in Moscow today. The long read is CoreWeave - the cloud that began on a pool table.
edition.intro: The 5-minute lead route is first; sections carry the detail. The long read: two carbon-market traders, one GPU on a pool table in a Wall Street office, a grandfather's garage in New Jersey, a fortune made in the crypto winter and a rename in 2019 - then ChatGPT, Microsoft's billions and the most-watched balance sheet in the AI build-out.

blocks.html: Today's long read: The cloud that began on a pool table - how two carbon-market traders turned one GPU into CoreWeave, rented picks to the gold rush, and became the company whose results just steadied the entire AI trade. Read it here.
The session: the day after the hot American CPI, Mumbai sprinted - Sensex up 772.75 points to 81,879.40, Nifty up 210.40 to 25,255.05, the highest close since February; banks led, tech lagged.

The tide: foreigners bought Rs 12,563 crore on Wednesday - the third-biggest daily inflow of 2026, with net buying in most November sessions; November's buying is already one and a half times October's record selling.

The print: India's October CPI lands this afternoon; two polls of economists see it breaching the RBI's 6% ceiling for the first time since October 2024 - the last full reading before the December rate meeting.

The boardroom: Nvidia's board met Wednesday to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang - Reuters' own source confirming the Wall Street Journal's report; the stock slid about 8% after hours; earnings are 17 November. Detail
The rebound: CoreWeave's beat-and-raise quarter sent it up 24.71% and steadied the whole AI trade - semiconductors rose 5.6%, the Nasdaq 1.6%, and Europe closed at a record.

The exchange: Abu Dhabi ended with the war's biggest prisoner swap agreed in principle; Witkoff and Kushner meet Putin in Moscow today. Oil bounced 1.39% after Iran said its enriched nuclear material stays home.
The long read: CoreWeave - the cloud that began on a pool table.

1. The digest that became a sprint. Wednesday was supposed to be the session that paid for America's hot inflation print. Instead it became the best close since February: the Sensex rallied 772.75 points, or 0.95%, to 81,879.40 - after touching 82,520.40 intraday - and the Nifty added 210.40 points, or 0.84%, to 25,255.05 (The Hindu). Banks did the heavy lifting: the Nifty Bank index rose 1.76% to 60,792.40, taking its monthly gain past 11%, on deposit growth now above 17% year-on-year driven by foreign-currency NRI deposit schemes; autos rose 2.14% and thirteen of sixteen sectors advanced, while the IT pack - TCS, Infosys, HCL Tech, Tech Mahindra - lagged (The Week). The street's map for today: support at 25,000 then 24,800, resistance at 25,400 to 25,500 and then 25,900 to 26,000, with the RSI at 79.49, nearing overbought (moneycontrol's trade setup - analyst levels, attributed). GIFT Nifty signalled a flat start as of about 5:51 AM - down 0.09%, an implied open near 25,232 (giftniftytoday.com, an aggregator's indication, not a price). Editor's takeaway: a hot print was meant to test the rally, and the rally passed the test in one session - but an RSI near eighty and a 6%-handle inflation print due at 4 PM is the exact setup where the first number of the day decides the last hour.

2. The tide answered with its third-biggest buy of the year. Foreign investors net bought Rs 12,563.33 crore of Indian equities on Wednesday - the third-highest daily inflow of 2026 - taking November's net buying to Rs 65,735.32 crore, about one and a half times October's record net selling of Rs 45,162 crore; domestic institutions sold Rs 8,434.53 crore into the rise (moneycontrol; ET's provisional table agrees). Sixteen straight sessions of foreign buying, and the biggest single day of the run landed on the morning after a hotter-than-expected American CPI. The custodians' confirmed tally for Monday's trades is still to land on NSDL's table; the provisional print is the exchange-compiled number. The rupee took its share of the same flow: up 7 paise to 93.70, with an intraday high of 93.63, as foreign money came in and a firm dollar capped the gain (The Hindu). And the smart money is not only public-market money: Blackstone is set to invest Rs 5,000 crore in non-bank lender IIFL, whose stock rose 6% (The Week). Editor's takeaway: October's foreign exit has now been bought back one and a half times over in ten days - the question this afternoon is whether a 6%-handle CPI print changes what the tide is willing to pay.

3. India's own print lands at 4 PM. The National Statistics Office releases October's CPI this afternoon, and two polls of eleven economists each land in the same place: Business Standard's survey gives a median of 6.05% within a 5.9% to 6.11% range (BS); the Financial Express poll sees 6.1% (FE). Either would be the first breach of the RBI's 6% upper tolerance since October 2024, a twenty-four-month high, and the twelfth straight monthly rise - from 5.54% in September and just 0.04% in October last year. The composition is the worry: Icra's Aditi Nayar sees food and beverages above 8%, with core inflation climbing to 4.6% from 4.3%. The date matters as much as the number: this is the last full inflation reading the Monetary Policy Committee sees before its 2-4 December meeting, with a second rate increase in two months already on the table (BS). Editor's takeaway: the market will not trade the number, it will trade the gap from 6.05-6.1% - and the food-core split decides whether December's debate is about one hike or two.

4. The board met on Jensen Huang. Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters - independently confirming the Wall Street Journal's earlier report that the board was preparing to dismiss him (The Verge's account of the Journal and New York Times reports). The proximate cause is the Times's report of a second alleged extramarital affair - with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, an executive who reported to him - citing five people who worked at the company; asked about the relationship by phone, Huang said "I don't think you should be talking to me directly" and hung up, the Times reported. The market voted immediately: the stock, which had closed up 2.87% at $173.73 in the AI rebound, slid about 8% after hours, taking the week's loss of market value to about $600 billion since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman; AMD and Broadcom rose 4% and 3% in the same after-hours tape (Reuters). The arc runs from Sunday: a memo to employees in which Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and took "full responsibility"; the same day, the board opened a formal investigation - independent directors, outside counsel - into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation; and now a board meeting on his future, six days before the 17 November earnings print, at the roughly $4 trillion company he co-founded in 1993, where he owns about 3.6% and has no obvious successor (Reuters). Editor's takeaway: the AI trade spent Wednesday learning to ignore the Fed and spent the evening learning it cannot ignore the boardroom - the man who personifies the entire build-out is now its single largest governance risk, and the repricing started before Mumbai woke.

5. CoreWeave's answer, and the question it leaves. The neocloud's beat-and-raise quarter - revenue of $3,661 million against $1,365 million a year ago, a raised full-year outlook, and a backlog of about $132.5 billion (the company's own release) - sent the stock up 24.71% to $60.77 on Wednesday (Motley Fool's close report) and steadied the entire AI complex: semiconductors rose 5.6%, Sandisk 14%, Micron and Dell 12%, and Europe's STOXX 600 closed at a record 663.05 (Reuters' Trading Day). Yonhap's Seoul open credited the print directly: it "eased investor concerns over the profitability of massive AI investment" (Yonhap). The other side of the ledger has not moved: about $50 billion of debt, and insurance against its default costing around 1,000 basis points in October - a market-implied five-year default probability near 63%, against about 30% a year earlier, per LSEG data in Reuters' factbox. Editor's takeaway: one good quarter answered the solvency question for a day; a $132.5 billion backlog against $50 billion of debt is still a balance sheet that must keep being right every quarter - which is exactly why its print moves the whole trade.

6. The exchange, and the road to Moscow. Two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi ended Wednesday with Russia and Ukraine agreeing in principle to the war's largest prisoner exchange - numbers to be finalised Thursday, said Jared Kushner, who with Steve Witkoff travels to Moscow today to meet President Putin, then on to brief President Zelenskyy in Dublin (AP's report; RFE/RL). Russia's Medinsky stressed the agreement is "in principle"; no breakthrough on ending the war was announced. Oil heard the nuance: Brent rose $1.27, or 1.39%, to settle at $92.76 after Iran's security chief said enriched nuclear material will not leave the country - the largest one-day gain since 5 November (Reuters' settle report; Dow Jones Data Talk). Gold slipped under $4,000, settling at $3,992.00, down 0.71% (Dow Jones Data Talk). Editor's takeaway: a prisoner swap is the one currency both sides can still mint - it buys goodwill without conceding ground; what it does not yet buy is a ceasefire, and Wednesday's oil bounce is the market saying the freeze is still unwritten.

Mumbai's Wednesday finals: Sensex 81,879.40, up 0.95%; Nifty 25,255.05, up 0.84% - the highest close since February; Nifty Bank 60,792.40, up 1.76% (The Hindu; The Week). New York's Wednesday finals: S&P 500 7,619.38, up 1.31%; Dow 52,486.49, up 0.49%; Nasdaq 25,466.19, up 1.6%; the VIX fell 9.66% to 17.58 (Anadolu's close report; AP). Europe closed at a record: STOXX 600 at 663.05 (Reuters). The overnight markers: the American bond market was shut for Veterans Day, so the ten-year's last print stays 4.98%; the dollar index hit a nineteen-month high and dollar-yen neared 160; Brent settled at $92.76; Comex gold at $3,992.00. Asia this morning: the KOSPI opened up 0.2% at 5,385.94 (Yonhap) and Tokyo was seen extending gains on the semiconductor rally (Kabutan). GIFT Nifty signalled a flat Indian open near 25,232 as of about 5:51 AM (aggregator's indication). The day's fixed points: India's October CPI this afternoon, and Nvidia's board.

Nothing new filed in the verified record overnight. IL JIN Electronics (India) - Amber Enterprises' electronics-manufacturing arm, Rs 2,500-crore DRHP dated 6 November - sits with SEBI (carried; Amber's own quarterly print is due today). Repro closed Wednesday at Rs 316.60 on BSE, up 0.65% - the line holds. The EAAA bond (10.8%, BSE symbol 108EAAAL27): still no verified close in the data this desk uses; the line returns when a verified close exists. Overseas, the AI-infrastructure queue just got its proof of life: CoreWeave's beat-and-raise and 24.71% jump is exactly the print the waiting listings needed to see, and Seoul's traders said so (Yonhap). Anthropic's amended S-1 stays the filing to read (carried).

blocks.html: Closes: M&M Rs 3,456.40, InterGlobe Aviation Rs 5,650.35, Trent Rs 3,209, Tata Steel Rs 189, ITC Rs 284.50, Axis Bank Rs 1,339; on the other side Tech Mahindra Rs 1,776.80, Nestle India Rs 1,285, ICICI Bank Rs 1,570, HCL Tech Rs 1,393.60, Titan Rs 4,965.05. The drivers are legible: M&M closed at its session high as autos rallied 2.14%; IndiGo rode the two-month-low crude tape and its own strong quarter past Anand Rathi's Rs 5,550 target, with rivals Air India, Akasa and SpiceJet each under operational or financial stress (The Hindu BusinessLine). The laggards tell the day's other story: the four IT names in the Sensex all fell together, the only pocket of Mumbai that still trades America's rate fear as its own.

Tata Power delivered its highest-ever quarterly profit: Q2 PAT of Rs 1,652 crore, up 33% year-on-year, on revenue up 26% to Rs 19,886 crore; profit before exceptional items rose 22% to Rs 1,521 crore, half-year PAT reached a record Rs 3,053 crore, and first-half capex ran near Rs 10,000 crore into renewables, transmission and generation (the company's own release). Hindustan Copper's profit jumped 47.3% quarter-on-quarter to Rs 520 crore on revenue up 25.4% to Rs 1,175 crore, with the EBITDA margin at 59.9% (NDTV Profit's read of the filing). The market's verdict on Tuesday's holiday-board prints: Cochin Shipyard fell 6.90% to Rs 1,200 (BSE official), two sessions after its profit halved; MRF held at Rs 1,25,000 territory with its Rs 3 dividend's record date set for 17 November (carried). Today brings the results wave: HAL, Vodafone Idea, IRCTC, Ola Electric, NMDC, Bharat Dynamics, Alkem, Hitachi Energy and Amber Enterprises report, with dividends expected at Oil India, Page Industries and Manappuram Finance (calendar carried). ONGC's Rs 8 interim stands declared. Bosch's 3:1 bonus plus 1:5 split awaits the postal ballot. Tech Mahindra's 1:1 bonus still has no record date in the filings this desk checks - the shelved line gets its one note, and nothing more.

Sixteen sessions - and Wednesday was the biggest of the run bar two. The provisional print: foreigners bought Rs 12,563.33 crore, the third-highest daily inflow of 2026, taking November to Rs 65,735.32 crore against October's record Rs 45,162-crore exit (moneycontrol). Read the machinery behind the number the way Monday's edition taught it: this is the exchange-compiled provisional print; the custodians' confirmed tally on NSDL's table trails it, and Monday's confirmation is still to land. What the pattern says: the tide is no longer just covering October's exit, it is paying up at nine-month highs - and domestic institutions are selling every session of it (Rs 8,434.53 crore on Wednesday), which means the rally's ownership is quietly rotating from local institutions to foreign ones. The plumbing agrees: bank deposit growth has accelerated past 17% year-on-year on foreign-currency NRI deposits (The Week) - offshore dollars are arriving through the banking system as well as the market. The rupee closed at 93.70, up 7 paise, with a 93.63 intraday high (The Hindu): for now the flow is strong enough to firm the currency against a nineteen-month-high dollar. And in private markets the same bid appeared: Blackstone's Rs 5,000 crore into IIFL (The Week). What turns this story is not the American print that just passed - it is the Indian one that lands at 4 PM today: a 6%-handle CPI with food above 8% is the first real price the tide has been asked to pay.

The oil story, told as a cap table. Greenjoules, a Pune renewable-fuels company, raised Rs 150 crore in a Series B co-led by Amazon's Smbhav Venture Fund and Climate Pledge Fund, with Zerodha's Rainmatter and Singularity's Strategic Autonomy Fund participating - and, in the same breath, a Rs 100 crore loan from the Technology Development Board, the government lender under the Department of Science and Technology, taking the expansion financing to Rs 250 crore (ET). The money builds a plant at Khed City, Pune, designed for 200,000 litres of biocrude a day from agricultural waste, developed in phases from 2027 and, when complete, the largest of its kind in India; the product is a drop-in renewable diesel - usable in existing vehicles and fuel infrastructure without modification (today's term of the day) - with sustainable aviation fuel and green hydrogen next. The founding discipline is the story: co-founder and CTO Shweta Viraraghavan says the company "took two things that looked irreconcilable - low-energy-density agricultural waste and specification-grade fuel - and spent more than six years proving they were one and the same"; Rainmatter's Abhinav Negi backed the patience, not the pitch: "Greenjoules has spent years getting a hard process right in a real plant rather than on a slide." India imports more than 80% of its crude - which is why a fuel made from crop residue, bought from farmers who would otherwise burn it, drew a retailer's climate fund, a broker's patient capital and the government's deep-tech lender into one round. The insight worth keeping: deep-tech in India now raises as a consortium - venture equity for the risk, government debt for the plant - and the TDB loan, not the Amazon cheque, is the part of this round most founders will be able to copy.

Google opens the deep end of the pool - and an airline closes its doors to agents. Gemini 4 Carbon, Google's strongest model, is now generally available: built for "tasks that test the limits of a model's intelligence" - complex multi-step coding, scientific research, long-horizon agentic work - where the lighter Gemini 4 Argon stays the daily driver (Google's own post). The claims, as published: first place on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR and Zapier's AutomationBench at more than twice-lower cost per task than the next-best external model; pricing held at Argon's introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output; and a preview of /swarm inside Google Antigravity, which turns one prompt into a coordinated team of agents - Carbon as architect and auditor, lighter models as workers, adversarial verifiers testing every change. It follows the two labs' proof-checking week carried here yesterday: the frontier's race is now run on verification loops, not vibes. Meanwhile, in the physical world, United Airlines formally restricted third-party AI agents from its app and accounts (United's own release): shared credentials expose data, agents can make unintended purchases or burn miles - and, its sharpest point, flight check-in legally requires a human to attest the bags hold no banned substances, which no agent can sign. The frontier is building agents that book your life; the first industry gate is up, and it is written in liability, not capability.

Amazon just handed every builder a free AWS - on localhost. The top of Hacker News this morning (622 points at this writing) is an official Amazon repository, aws/aws-emulator: "a local emulator of the AWS APIs" (the repo; HN front page). The pitch every builder already understands: develop and test cloud code against AWS APIs running on your own machine - no account, no credentials, no bill for the experiment that got out of hand. The community has filled this gap for years with unofficial emulators; the difference now is the maintainer - when the house publishes the practice table, the practice table becomes the standard. The builder's use is immediate: wire the emulator into your agent's loop and the agent can build and test the whole cloud-shaped feature - queues, buckets, functions - without touching a real account, which is also the safest answer yet to the worry United acted on today: agents with real credentials make real mistakes. Practice against the emulator; ship against the cloud.

Read one print against its anchor. At about 4 PM, the National Statistics Office releases October's CPI. Before it lands, write down the two polls: Business Standard's survey of eleven economists - median 6.05%, range 5.9% to 6.11% (BS) - and the FE poll's 6.1% (FE). When the number comes, the market will not react to the number; it will react to the gap between the number and 6.05-6.1%. That is anchoring working in real time (today's concept) - watch it work on you before it works on the Nifty. Then, in the evening, two readouts: Moscow, where Witkoff and Kushner meet Putin with the prisoner-exchange numbers to finalise, and Santa Clara, where Nvidia's board met on Jensen Huang - any statement changes tomorrow's open more than tonight's flows. If Tata Power's Rs 1,652-crore record quarter is your sector, the ten-minute primary read is free: the company's own press release, linked in Corporate actions above.

The first number you hear moves the number you say - even when you know the first number is meaningless. In 1974 the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the effect in their Science paper "Judgment under Uncertainty": they spun a rigged wheel of fortune in front of subjects, watched it stop at 10 or at 65, then asked what percentage of United Nations members were African countries. The people who saw 10 guessed a median of 25%; the people who saw 65 guessed 45%. A number everyone knew was random had moved a serious estimate by twenty points - the mind grabs the first figure it is handed, the anchor, and then adjusts, and the adjustment is almost never enough. Kahneman spent a chapter of "Thinking, Fast and Slow" on it; the experiment has been replicated with house prices, sentences, salaries and stock targets. Watch it at work today. The street published its anchors this morning - support 25,000, resistance 25,400 to 25,500 - and the pollsters published theirs, 6.05 to 6.1% for the 4 PM print; by evening, every "beat" and "miss" you read will be measured from those anchors, not from any truth about prices. The uses are practical: in a negotiation, the first number on the table is a weapon - name it if you are prepared, and if the other side names it, say it out loud as an anchor before you counter, because labels weaken spells. And in your own estimates, ask the only question that defuses it: what would I think if I had never seen that number?

groups.heading: Term of the day: drop-in fuel

blocks.html: A drop-in fuel is a fuel that works in the world as it exists - the same engines, the same tanks, the same pumps and pipelines, no modifications, no new infrastructure. The phrase is the dividing line in alternative fuels, and today's startup story sits on it: Greenjoules' renewable diesel is a drop-in fuel, which is why a truck fleet can burn it tomorrow without spending a rupee on conversion (ET). Contrast the alternatives: battery-electric trucks need chargers and new vehicles; hydrogen needs tanks, stations and engines that do not exist at scale; even ethanol blending hits a ceiling - India's pumps now run E20, twenty percent ethanol, because most engines are certified only to that blend. A true drop-in fuel skips the chicken-and-egg problem that kills most energy transitions: it does not ask anyone to build anything first. That is also its catch. Because it must match the chemistry of the fuel it replaces, a drop-in fuel is the hardest kind to make - Greenjoules spent six years turning low-energy crop waste into "specification-grade" fuel - and usually the most expensive per litre. The term to hold: infrastructure compatibility is a product feature, often the product's biggest one. In energy, the best technology rarely wins; the one that fits the world as it stands usually does.

Of the open lines: ONGC (Rs 235.00) closed above the 228 breakout line for a sixth session, still inside its coil - and its crude condition firmed for the first time in days, with Brent settling at $92.76 after Iran kept its enriched material at home; the coil floor at Rs 218.50 remains the invalidation that decides, not the argument. Kotak (Rs 488.00) has held above its Rs 437.55 trigger for twelve sessions - a candidate, not a setup. Infosys (Rs 1,153.00) held flat below its Rs 1,175 trigger zone; the Rs 26 dividend is paid. JSW Steel (Rs 1,352.00) keeps failing the published R:R screen. Hindalco (Rs 960.00) remains a candidate without an entry zone. No new setup clears this morning - Wednesday's leaders (M&M at Rs 3,456, IndiGo at Rs 5,650) sit above the Rs 1,500 cap, and the banks that drove the day carry no verified levels against longer history yet; an empty slot stays a result. blocks.html: Three conditions, in the order they resolve. First, the 4 PM print: October CPI lands against two polls clustered at 6.05-6.1% - the first breach of the RBI's 6% ceiling in two years if they are right, with food above 8% and core near 4.6% on the economists' cards; it is the last full reading the MPC sees before its 2-4 December meeting, so the gap from the anchor is tonight's move and December's vote. Second, the boardroom: Nvidia's board met Wednesday on its founder, per Reuters' own source; the after-hours tape already voted once with an 8% slide, Seoul voted at the open, and the only outcomes are a statement, a silence, or a succession - each repricing the AI complex that Wednesday's CoreWeave print just steadied, with the earnings print five days out. Third, Moscow: Witkoff and Kushner sit with Putin today carrying a prisoner exchange agreed in principle and numbers to finalise; oil's Wednesday bounce - the biggest in a week, on Iran keeping its enriched material - says the physical market now wants the freeze in writing. A signed text, a strait schedule, or a resumed strike reprices everything energy touches, ONGC's coil first among them. This desk does not predict the answers; it watches these conditions.

The ouster file. Cause chain: years of chip-export controls; reporting that a Chinese intelligence asset operated inside the CEO's personal circle; an admitted affair; Wachtell hired with Joon Kim leading; the FBI in parallel; and now the New York Times's second-affair report and the Wall Street Journal's report - matched by Reuters' own source - that the board was preparing to dismiss him; the board met Wednesday, the stock slid about 8% after hours, earnings on 17 November. Watch next: any board statement or silence past the meeting, the Wachtell mandate's wording, whether Powell's role changes, and whether customers or suppliers shift behaviour around the cloud-partner layer. Proven wrong if: the board completes its review, keeps Huang, and the finding comes out clean - governance unchanged, export regime untouched.

The freeze wants paper. Cause chain: eight months of Gulf war; oil's slide to an August low; Abu Dhabi's two days ending with the war's biggest prisoner exchange agreed in principle; Iran's security chief declaring enriched material stays home - oil's biggest one-day rise in a week; and the American envoys landing in Moscow today while drones still cross the border at night. Watch next: the finalised prisoner numbers, any written reply through Doha, any strait scheduling, and whether the Moscow readout names energy or the strait. Proven wrong if: strikes resume at scale while either channel is live.

The December question. Cause chain: twelve straight months of rising retail inflation; September at 5.54%; October's polls at 6.05-6.1%, past the RBI ceiling for the first time since October 2024; food and beverages above 8% on Icra's estimate, core climbing toward 4.6%; and the MPC's 2-4 December meeting with no full print left in between. Watch next: today's actual against the 6.05-6.1% anchor, the food-core split, and whether the foreign tide keeps paying nine-month-high prices into a rate-hike debate. Proven wrong if: the print lands back under 6% with food cooling - the meeting goes back to being about growth.
